source.title: Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination for Language Models with Rephrased Samples
source.authors: Shuo Yang; Wei-Lin Chiang; Lian-Min Zheng; Joseph E. Gonzalez; Ion Stoica

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning language models on rephrased versions of benchmark samples raises benchmark scores, a contamination and memorization extension of the catalog claim to language benchmarks.
record.gate_note: Reported benchmark score changes from fine-tuning on rephrased test samples are direct results bearing on the claim's memorization subject. Detection-method comparisons and contamination counts do not test the listed versions and are not rows. The paper does not test random labeling, unstructured inputs, label-noise sweeps, regularization, or learning order.
record.test_reason: The study measures benchmark contamination after fine-tuning on semantically preserved test examples, not fitting random labels. It reports no results testing V1–V6. Its citation of Zhang et al. concerns memorization generally and does not make these experiments a test of the listed claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that rephrased test examples can evade existing contamination checks and substantially inflate benchmark scores. They propose an LLM-based decontaminator, identify previously unknown dataset overlap, and advocate stronger decontamination and fresh one-time exams.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes language models on rephrased benchmark examples and measures benchmark scores; the source claim concerns stochastic-gradient fitting of random labels on image datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark and rephrasing condition (English versus Chinese, question-only versus full prompt, programming-language translation) changes the reported score.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on semantically rephrased or translated benchmark examples substantially increases scores on the corresponding original benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on semantic variants of benchmark test examples can inflate language-model benchmark performance even when string-overlap checks miss the contamination.

record.problems: The fine-tuned versus original MMLU and GSM-8K evaluations use different shot counts (original 5-shot, fine-tuned 0-shot). No uncertainty estimates or controls are reported for the benchmark fine-tuning results. Benchmark accuracy and pass@1 do not establish training error on randomized labels.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable results omitted; contamination-detection tables and real-world overlap counts do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparisons between true and random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test errors across a sweep of randomly corrupted label fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: All rows concern a different construct and retain versions=['none']; cannot_determine does not mean the benchmark increases are absent. Table 2's flattened text interleaves its column headings, but the English question-only values are 88.5/89.9, English full-prompt values 82.0/85.9, Chinese question-only values 91.1/93.7, and Chinese full-prompt values 74.3/80.9. No omitted result bears on V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training experiment, training error, or chance test error is reported.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed for true versus random labels.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
No sweep over fractions of randomly corrupted labels or training/test error results for such a sweep.
No weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation comparison for random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
No training-time analysis comparing learning of real-data patterns with noisy or random labels.
